docs.title: ZodiacCore Go
docs.text: Build Go services with consistent configuration, API responses, and request logs.

docs.title: Choose your starting point
docs.text:
Your situation Start here You are building a new service Create a project, then add a business endpoint You already have a Go application Use ZodiacCore in an existing application You need to change a service setting Configure your application You need to find the logs for a request Write and correlate logs

A generated project uses Cobra for commands, Fx for dependency injection, and chi with Huma for HTTP APIs.

In an existing application, import the packages you need. Configuration and logging can be used without a web server; the HTTP middleware accepts net/http handlers. The typed API helpers integrate with Huma.

docs.title: What a client receives
docs.text:
A successful business endpoint returns data inside a standard response:

{"code":0,"data":{"id":1,"title":"Cannot sign in"},"message":"Success"}

Endpoints can return public business errors with an HTTP status and message. Request IDs connect a client's response to the service's logs. Huma generates OpenAPI documentation from the endpoint's input and output types.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text: See pkg.go.dev for types and functions. Choose the version used by your application's go.mod in both the API reference and this site's version selector. dev describes the development version.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
All notable changes to this project are documented in this file.

The format is based on Keep a Changelog, and this project adheres to Semantic Versioning.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Generated services include an in-memory user module at internal/user, with GET /users and GET /users/{id}.
  • humatransport.NewError and humatransport.NewErrorWithContext integrate Huma framework errors with Zodiac responses and request logging.
  • Usage guides cover XML requests and raw XML, HTML, CSV, text, and binary responses. A WebSocket example demonstrates message handling and shutdown, including upgrades in progress.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Generated services place the command in cmd/<name> and compose feature Fx modules from internal/app. HTTP setup lives in internal/httpserver; run newly generated services with go run ./cmd/<name> serve.
  • Huma errors use the code/data/message envelope, with client error details in data.errors. Generated services install the error factories at startup; existing applications must assign huma.NewError = humatransport.NewError and huma.NewErrorWithContext = humatransport.NewErrorWithContext before creating APIs to apply this format to framework errors. These factories affect all Huma APIs in the process.
  • Error documentation follows Huma's native Errors and Responses rules; an entry in Errors overrides Responses for the same status.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • Error normalization preserves response headers carried by wrapped errors and logs internal error causes without including those causes in responses.
Initial release. Requires Go 1.26.0 or newer.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• zodiac new generates standalone services with Cobra commands, Fx dependency injection, chi/Huma APIs, a health endpoint, and graceful shutdown.
  • Layered YAML configuration supports environment selection, configurable search paths, explicit environment variable bindings, strict struct decoding, and application validation.
  • Generic code/data/message responses and public business errors integrate with Huma and OpenAPI while preserving Huma's native validation responses.
  • HTTP middleware provides request IDs, access logs, panic recovery, and request metadata shared through context.
  • JSON logging uses slog with configurable levels and request and service metadata.
  • Usage guides, versioned documentation, and CI checks cover the library and generated services across Go 1.26 and 1.27.

docs.title: CLI installation and options
docs.text: Use zodiac new to generate an application.

docs.title: Install and generate
docs.text:
go install github.com/TTWShell/zodiac-core/cmd/zodiac@latest
zodiac new myapp --module example.com/myapp

For a versioned installation, replace @latest with an available version from Releases. Go installs the executable into GOBIN, or GOPATH/bin when GOBIN is unset; include that directory in your PATH.

A version-installed CLI records its own ZodiacCore version in the generated project's go.mod. Without release tags, Go may resolve @latest to a pseudo-version.

docs.title: Choose a directory or dependency version
docs.text:
zodiac new <name> --module <module-path> [flags]
Flag When to use it --module Set the new application's Go module path; required --output, -o Write somewhere other than ./<name> --core-version Select a particular available ZodiacCore version for the application --core-path Set a local ZodiacCore module path using a replace directive

For example, generate into a separate application directory:

zodiac new myapp --module example.com/myapp --output ../services/myapp

Names must start with a lowercase letter and contain lowercase letters, digits, and single hyphens. Output directories must be absent or empty. The generator rejects existing files and symbolic-link destinations.

Run go mod tidy inside the generated project to download its dependencies.

docs.title: Run the generated application's commands
docs.text:
From the application's directory:

APPLICATION_ENVIRONMENT=develop go run ./cmd/myapp serve --config-dir ./config

--config-dir defaults to config, relative to the current working directory. For the myapp project, MYAPP_HTTP_ADDR overrides the listener address. Other project names use an uppercase prefix with hyphens replaced by underscores.

Add new application commands in cmd/myapp/, following the existing serve.go pattern. Use zodiac --help for generator commands and go run ./cmd/myapp --help for application commands.

docs.title: Configure your application
docs.text: Use configuration files for shared settings and explicit environment bindings for values that vary between deployments. This guide uses the myapp project from Create a service.

docs.title: Select an environment
docs.text:
APPLICATION_ENVIRONMENT=develop go run ./cmd/myapp serve --config-dir ./config

This loads shared files such as config/app.yaml, then matching overrides such as config/app.develop.yaml. When APPLICATION_ENVIRONMENT is unset or empty, the environment is production.

develop, testing, staging, and production are standard names. Custom names are also allowed: start with a letter and use letters, digits, underscores, or hyphens. Names are normalized to lowercase.

The configuration directory is relative to the current working directory. For an installed service, you can use an absolute path:

APPLICATION_ENVIRONMENT=production ./bin/myapp serve --config-dir /etc/myapp

docs.title: Add a business setting
docs.text:
The ticket example needs a support team name. In internal/config/config.go, add SupportConfig and replace the existing Config declaration with:

type SupportConfig struct {
    Team string `mapstructure:"team"`
}

type Config struct {
    HTTP    HTTPConfig         `mapstructure:"http"`
    Support SupportConfig      `mapstructure:"support"`
    Env     zconfig.Environment `mapstructure:"-"`
}

Keep the file's existing imports, HTTPConfig, and loading function. Append this setting to config/app.yaml, keeping the existing http settings:

support:
  team: "general"

docs.title: Allow an environment override
docs.text:
In the same file's Load function, update EnvBindings to include the new key:

EnvBindings: map[string]string{
    "http.addr":    "MYAPP_HTTP_ADDR",
    "support.team": "MYAPP_SUPPORT_TEAM",
},

Restart with an override:

APPLICATION_ENVIRONMENT=develop MYAPP_SUPPORT_TEAM=priority go run ./cmd/myapp serve

The effective team is now priority. An unbound environment variable does not change configuration; an empty binding value falls back to the file value.

APPLICATION_ENVIRONMENT is reserved for selecting which files to load. Do not use it as a business setting's environment binding.

docs.title: Reject invalid settings at startup
docs.text:
Add this check inside the existing (*Config).Validate method, before its final return nil:

if c.Support.Team == "" {
    return errors.New("support.team is required")
}

Validation runs after file and environment values are decoded. An invalid configuration prevents the generated server from starting. Keep the existing HTTP checks.

docs.title: Understand overrides
docs.text:
The effective value is determined in this order, with later values taking precedence:

  1. Base YAML files, such as app.yaml.
  2. Matching environment files, such as app.production.yaml.
  3. Nonempty values from explicitly bound environment variables.

Within each file group, directories follow SearchPaths order and filenames follow lexical order. Files in subdirectories are not loaded. An environment file is optional, but at least one matching configuration file must exist.

Maps merge by key. Lists and scalar values replace earlier values. Explicit null resets the destination field to its Go zero value. Unknown configuration fields and values that cannot decode into the declared Go types are errors.

docs.title: Use configuration without the generator
docs.text:
In an existing application, define your own struct and call the public loader:

package settings

import (
    "errors"

    "github.com/TTWShell/zodiac-core/config"
)

type Config struct {
    Support struct {
        Team string `mapstructure:"team"`
    } `mapstructure:"support"`
}

func (c *Config) Validate() error {
    if c.Support.Team == "" {
        return errors.New("support.team is required")
    }
    return nil
}

func Load(directory string) (*Config, error) {
    return config.Load[Config](config.Options{
        SearchPaths: []string{directory},
        EnvBindings: map[string]string{
            "support.team": "MYAPP_SUPPORT_TEAM",
        },
    })
}

For this standalone example, create a YAML file containing only the support setting shown above. When adapting it to your application, declare all the settings your files contain.

Use config.Read followed by source.Decode(&cfg) when you need to populate an existing struct with defaults. Missing fields retain those defaults. Settings are read at startup; restart the application to apply file or environment changes. See the configuration reference for section decoding and file discovery.

docs.title: Use ZodiacCore in an existing application
docs.text:
You can adopt configuration, logging, or HTTP helpers separately.

From your application's Go module:

go get github.com/TTWShell/zodiac-core@latest

Requires Go 1.26.0 or newer.

docs.title: Add configuration or logging
docs.text:
For configuration, define your application settings and load them using config.Load. The standalone configuration example includes validation and an environment override.

For logging, create a logger at startup and pass it to your application's constructors:

logger := logging.New("myapp", slog.LevelInfo)

Import log/slog and github.com/TTWShell/zodiac-core/logging. See logging to set the process default or use a different output. Neither package requires Fx or an HTTP server.

docs.title: Add an HTTP API with chi and Huma
docs.text:
Create internal/httpapi/http.go to provide a handler for your existing server:

package httpapi

import (
    "context"
    "log/slog"
    "net/http"

    "github.com/danielgtaylor/huma/v2"
    "github.com/danielgtaylor/huma/v2/adapters/humachi"
    "github.com/go-chi/chi/v5"

    "github.com/TTWShell/zodiac-core/response"
    httptransport "github.com/TTWShell/zodiac-core/transport/http"
    humatransport "github.com/TTWShell/zodiac-core/transport/huma"
)

type Ticket struct {
    ID    int    `json:"id"`
    Title string `json:"title"`
}

type GetTicketInput struct {
    ID int `path:"id" minimum:"1"`
}

func NewHandler(logger *slog.Logger) http.Handler {
    huma.NewError = humatransport.NewError
    huma.NewErrorWithContext = humatransport.NewErrorWithContext
    router := chi.NewRouter()
    router.Use(httptransport.Middleware(httptransport.Options{
        Logger: logger, ServiceName: "myapp",
    }))
    router.NotFound(httptransport.ErrorHandler(http.StatusNotFound))
    api := humachi.New(router, humatransport.DefaultConfig("My App", "1.0.0"))
    humatransport.Register(api, huma.Operation{
        OperationID: "get-ticket",
        Method:      http.MethodGet,
        Path:        "/tickets/{id}",
        Errors:      []int{http.StatusNotFound},
    }, func(ctx context.Context, input *GetTicketInput) (*Ticket, error) {
        if input.ID != 1 {
            return nil, response.NewError(http.StatusNotFound, "Ticket not found")
        }
        logger.InfoContext(ctx, "Ticket retrieved", "ticket_id", input.ID)
        return &Ticket{ID: 1, Title: "Cannot sign in"}, nil
    })
    return router
}

Run go mod tidy after adding the file. In your server's constructor, use httpapi.NewHandler(logger) as its Handler. Import internal/httpapi using your application's module path. Keep your server's existing listener, timeouts, and shutdown handling.

To use Zodiac error responses, assign both error factories once at startup, before creating APIs or serving requests. They apply to all Huma APIs in the process. Generated projects include this setup.

Once that server is running, request /tickets/1 for the sample ticket and /tickets/2 for a public 404. Interactive API documentation is served at /docs. The ticket tutorial shows how to inject a business service when using Fx.

docs.title: Keep an existing router
docs.text:
For an existing chi router, install httptransport.Middleware before registering routes, create the Huma API with humachi.New, and register your new operations on that API.

For another net/http router, the middleware can wrap its handler directly:

handler := httptransport.Middleware(httptransport.Options{
    Logger: logger, ServiceName: "myapp",
})(existingHandler)

This adds request metadata, access logging, and panic recovery. It does not change the successful response bodies produced by your existing handlers. To use typed responses and OpenAPI, construct a Huma API with an appropriate router adapter and register operations through humatransport.Register.

docs.title: Create a service
docs.text: Requires Go 1.26.0 or newer.

docs.title: Install the project generator
docs.text:
go install github.com/TTWShell/zodiac-core/cmd/zodiac@latest

Make sure Go's binary installation directory is on your PATH: GOBIN if set, otherwise the bin directory under GOPATH (usually $HOME/go/bin).

For a specific version, see CLI installation and versions.

docs.title: Create your project
docs.text:
zodiac new myapp --module example.com/myapp
cd myapp
go mod tidy

myapp is the project name. example.com/myapp is the Go module path used throughout this tutorial; replace it with your repository's module path in your own project, including in the examples' imports.

The generator creates a new myapp directory. It must be absent or empty.

docs.title: Start the service
docs.text:
APPLICATION_ENVIRONMENT=develop go run ./cmd/myapp serve

Check it from another terminal:

curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8080/health

You should receive HTTP 200, an X-Request-ID response header, and this body:

{"code":0,"data":{"status":"ok"},"message":"Success"}

Visit http://127.0.0.1:8080/docs to try endpoints in your browser. The OpenAPI document is available at /openapi.json. Press Ctrl+C to stop the service.

If port 8080 is occupied, choose another address:

APPLICATION_ENVIRONMENT=develop MYAPP_HTTP_ADDR=127.0.0.1:9090 go run ./cmd/myapp serve

docs.title: Add your first business endpoint
docs.text: Follow the ticket endpoint tutorial to add a service and route.

docs.title: Build an executable
docs.text:
go build -o bin/myapp ./cmd/myapp
APPLICATION_ENVIRONMENT=production ./bin/myapp serve --config-dir ./config

Ship the configuration directory with the binary, or supply another directory with --config-dir. The generated production configuration listens on :8080. Use configuration to set environment-specific values and bind environment variables for deployment.

docs.title: Add a business endpoint
docs.text:
Add GET /tickets/{id} to the myapp project from Create a service. A client will receive a ticket, a 404 when it does not exist, or a validation error when its ID is invalid.

First, follow Add a business setting to define cfg.Support.Team, add its YAML value, and bind MYAPP_SUPPORT_TEAM.

docs.title: Write the ticket service and route
docs.text:
Create internal/tickets/tickets.go with the following contents. The example contains one read-only sample ticket so you can try the API without a database.

package tickets

import (
    "context"
    "log/slog"
    "net/http"

    "github.com/danielgtaylor/huma/v2"

    "github.com/TTWShell/zodiac-core/response"
    humatransport "github.com/TTWShell/zodiac-core/transport/huma"
)

type Ticket struct {
    ID    int    `json:"id"`
    Title string `json:"title"`
    Team  string `json:"team"`
}

type Service struct {
    logger  *slog.Logger
    tickets map[int]Ticket
}

func NewService(team string, logger *slog.Logger) *Service {
    return &Service{
        logger: logger,
        tickets: map[int]Ticket{
            1: {ID: 1, Title: "Cannot sign in", Team: team},
        },
    }
}

func (s *Service) Get(ctx context.Context, id int) (*Ticket, error) {
    ticket, ok := s.tickets[id]
    if !ok {
        return nil, response.NewError(http.StatusNotFound, "Ticket not found")
    }
    s.logger.InfoContext(ctx, "Ticket retrieved", "ticket_id", id)
    return &ticket, nil
}

type GetInput struct {
    ID int `path:"id" minimum:"1"`
}

func Register(api huma.API, service *Service) {
    humatransport.Register(api, huma.Operation{
        OperationID: "get-ticket",
        Method:      http.MethodGet,
        Path:        "/tickets/{id}",
        Summary:     "Get a ticket",
        Errors:      []int{http.StatusNotFound},
    }, func(ctx context.Context, input *GetInput) (*Ticket, error) {
        return service.Get(ctx, input.ID)
    })
}

The handler returns business data. Register supplies the response envelope and exposes the input and output types in OpenAPI.

docs.title: Connect the service to your application
docs.text:
Create internal/tickets/module.go:

package tickets

import (
    "log/slog"

    "go.uber.org/fx"

    "example.com/myapp/internal/config"
)

func newService(cfg *config.Config, logger *slog.Logger) *Service {
    return NewService(cfg.Support.Team, logger)
}

var Module = fx.Module("tickets",
    fx.Provide(newService),
    fx.Invoke(Register),
)

In internal/app/app.go, add this import:

"example.com/myapp/internal/tickets"

Add tickets.Module inside the existing fx.New(...) call, keeping its current options:

tickets.Module,

docs.title: Try the endpoint
docs.text:
Start the application from its project directory:

APPLICATION_ENVIRONMENT=develop MYAPP_SUPPORT_TEAM=priority go run ./cmd/myapp serve

Request the sample ticket:

curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8080/tickets/1

HTTP 200:

{"code":0,"data":{"id":1,"title":"Cannot sign in","team":"priority"},"message":"Success"}

Request a ticket that does not exist:

curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8080/tickets/2

HTTP 404:

{"code":404,"data":null,"message":"Ticket not found"}

Request /tickets/0 to receive HTTP 422:

{"code":422,"data":{"errors":[{"message":"expected number >= 1","location":"path.id","value":0}]},"message":"validation failed"}

Visit http://127.0.0.1:8080/docs to see and call the new operation.

The successful request also emits a Ticket retrieved log with ticket_id and request_id. Compare the latter with the response's X-Request-ID header. See logging for recording additional business events.

docs.title: Return other results
Return XML or other formats
docs.text:
Use RegisterOutput with a Content-Type header and a []byte body to send XML, HTML, CSV, or binary data. The bytes are sent as-is, without a JSON envelope.

To add an XML export to the ticket example, import encoding/xml in internal/tickets/tickets.go and add these types:

type ticketXML struct {
    XMLName xml.Name `xml:"ticket"`
    ID      int      `xml:"id"`
    Title   string   `xml:"title"`
    Team    string   `xml:"team"`
}

type xmlOutput struct {
    ContentType string `header:"Content-Type"`
    Body        []byte
}

Add this registration inside the existing Register function:

humatransport.RegisterOutput(api, huma.Operation{
    OperationID: "export-ticket-xml",
    Method:      http.MethodGet,
    Path:        "/tickets/{id}/xml",
    Errors:      []int{http.StatusNotFound},
    Responses: map[string]*huma.Response{
        "200": {
            Description: "Ticket as XML",
            Content: map[string]*huma.MediaType{
                "application/xml": {Schema: &huma.Schema{Type: "string"}},
            },
        },
    },
}, func(ctx context.Context, input *GetInput) (*xmlOutput, error) {
    ticket, err := service.Get(ctx, input.ID)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    body, err := xml.Marshal(ticketXML{
        ID: ticket.ID, Title: ticket.Title, Team: ticket.Team,
    })
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    return &xmlOutput{ContentType: "application/xml", Body: body}, nil
})

Restart the service and request the export:

curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8080/tickets/1/xml

The response has HTTP 200 and Content-Type: application/xml:

<ticket><id>1</id><title>Cannot sign in</title><team>priority</team></ticket>

The handler selects the format by writing those bytes. Sending Accept: application/xml to the JSON ticket endpoint does not change its response. With the default API configuration, a missing ticket or invalid ID still returns the Zodiac JSON error envelope.

For other formats, use the same output shape with the corresponding bytes and content type, such as text/html, text/csv, or application/octet-stream. Declare that media type in Responses so OpenAPI describes the response clients actually receive.

If an endpoint also accepts XML, name that media type on the raw body and decode it in the handler:

type xmlInput struct {
    RawBody []byte `contentType:"application/xml"`
}

Decode RawBody with xml.Unmarshal and validate the result in the handler. Huma does not validate that XML. Return response.NewError(http.StatusBadRequest, "invalid XML") for malformed XML. Without the contentType tag, OpenAPI describes the request as application/octet-stream.

docs.title: Write and correlate logs
docs.text: Use a single application logger and pass each request's context when recording business events.

docs.title: Use the logger in a generated service
docs.text:
The generated application provides a *slog.Logger through Fx. Receive it in your constructor, as shown in the ticket service.

Inside a request, record what happened with InfoContext, WarnContext, or ErrorContext:

s.logger.InfoContext(ctx, "Ticket retrieved", "ticket_id", id)

Request logs include request_id and service automatically.

docs.title: Find the logs for a request
docs.text:
Make a request and inspect its response headers:

curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8080/tickets/1

Find X-Request-ID in the response and search your log destination for that value in the request_id field. The ticket event and access log share the same ID. Access logs include the method, path, HTTP status, and duration in milliseconds.

Logs are written as JSON to stderr.

docs.title: Change the log level
docs.text:
In a generated application's cmd/myapp/main.go, select the minimum severity when creating the logger:

logger := logging.New("myapp", slog.LevelDebug)

Import log/slog and github.com/TTWShell/zodiac-core/logging in an existing application. Use slog.LevelInfo, slog.LevelWarn, or slog.LevelError for other thresholds; nil defaults to INFO.

If your application needs to change the threshold while running, retain a *slog.LevelVar and pass it to logging.New:

var level slog.LevelVar
logger := logging.New("myapp", &level)
level.Set(slog.LevelDebug)

docs.title: Initialize logging in an existing application
docs.text:
Create the logger in your application's entry point:

logger := logging.New("myapp", slog.LevelInfo)
slog.SetDefault(logger)

SetDefault is needed when your application uses package-level functions such as slog.InfoContext. Pass the logger to components that receive their dependencies explicitly. Install the HTTP middleware to make request metadata available.

docs.title: Choose another output format or destination
docs.text:
Use a standard slog handler and wrap it to retain request metadata:

handler := slog.NewTextHandler(os.Stderr, &slog.HandlerOptions{
    Level: slog.LevelInfo,
})
logger := slog.New(requestctx.NewLogHandler(handler, "myapp"))

Import os and github.com/TTWShell/zodiac-core/requestctx for this example. Pass another io.Writer in place of os.Stderr to change the destination. See slog for handler options.

docs.title: Add a WebSocket endpoint
docs.text:
Add an echo endpoint to the myapp project from Create a service. This example uses coder/websocket with the generated Chi adapter. Text and binary messages are echoed unchanged.

From the project directory, install the dependency:

go get github.com/coder/websocket@v1.8.15

docs.title: Write the handler
docs.text:
Create internal/echo/echo.go:

package echo

import (
    "context"
    "net/http"
    "sync"

    "github.com/coder/websocket"
    "github.com/danielgtaylor/huma/v2"
    "github.com/danielgtaylor/huma/v2/adapters/humachi"

    httptransport "github.com/TTWShell/zodiac-core/transport/http"
    humatransport "github.com/TTWShell/zodiac-core/transport/huma"
)

type Handler struct {
    mu       sync.Mutex
    handlers sync.WaitGroup
    stopping bool
    conns    map[*websocket.Conn]struct{}
}

func NewHandler() *Handler {
    return &Handler{conns: make(map[*websocket.Conn]struct{})}
}

func (h *Handler) Register(api huma.API) {
    humatransport.RegisterOutput(api, huma.Operation{
        OperationID:   "echo-websocket",
        Method:        http.MethodGet,
        Path:          "/ws/echo",
        DefaultStatus: http.StatusSwitchingProtocols,
        Hidden:        true,
    }, func(context.Context, *struct{}) (*huma.StreamResponse, error) {
        return &huma.StreamResponse{Body: h.serve}, nil
    })
}

func (h *Handler) serve(ctx huma.Context) {
    r, w := humachi.Unwrap(ctx)
    h.mu.Lock()
    if h.stopping {
        h.mu.Unlock()
        httptransport.ErrorHandler(http.StatusServiceUnavailable)(w, r)
        return
    }
    // Admission and shutdown share the lock, so no Add can race with Stop's Wait.
    h.handlers.Add(1)
    h.mu.Unlock()
    defer h.handlers.Done()

    conn, err := websocket.Accept(w, r, nil)
    if err != nil {
        return
    }
    defer conn.CloseNow()

    h.mu.Lock()
    if h.stopping {
        h.mu.Unlock()
        _ = conn.Close(websocket.StatusGoingAway, "server shutting down")
        return
    }
    h.conns[conn] = struct{}{}
    h.mu.Unlock()
    defer func() {
        h.mu.Lock()
        delete(h.conns, conn)
        h.mu.Unlock()
    }()

    conn.SetReadLimit(64 * 1024)
    for {
        kind, data, err := conn.Read(r.Context())
        if err != nil {
            return
        }
        if err := conn.Write(r.Context(), kind, data); err != nil {
            return
        }
    }
}

func (h *Handler) Stop(ctx context.Context) error {
    h.mu.Lock()
    h.stopping = true
    conns := make([]*websocket.Conn, 0, len(h.conns))
    for conn := range h.conns {
        conns = append(conns, conn)
    }
    h.mu.Unlock()

    for _, conn := range conns {
        go func() {
            _ = conn.Close(websocket.StatusGoingAway, "server shutting down")
        }()
    }
    done := make(chan struct{})
    go func() {
        h.handlers.Wait()
        close(done)
    }()
    select {
    case <-done:
        return nil
    case <-ctx.Done():
        return ctx.Err()
    }
}

RegisterOutput passes control to the stream callback. humachi.Unwrap obtains the HTTP request and writer needed by websocket.Accept. The endpoint is hidden from OpenAPI because its messages are WebSocket frames, not HTTP response bodies.

docs.title: Connect the module
docs.text:
Create internal/echo/module.go:

package echo

import (
    "github.com/danielgtaylor/huma/v2"
    "go.uber.org/fx"
)

var Module = fx.Module("echo",
    fx.Provide(NewHandler),
    fx.Invoke(func(api huma.API, handler *Handler, lifecycle fx.Lifecycle) {
        handler.Register(api)
        lifecycle.Append(fx.Hook{OnStop: handler.Stop})
    }),
)

In internal/app/app.go, import example.com/myapp/internal/echo and add echo.Module after httpserver.Module in the existing fx.New(...) call.

The stop hook sends close code 1001 (going away) to active clients and waits for their close handshakes until the stop context expires. If it expires, the hook returns the context error; unfinished handshakes remain subject to the WebSocket library's timeouts. Upgrades already in progress are included in the wait and close with 1001; new upgrade requests receive HTTP 503. This hook is necessary because http.Server.Shutdown does not close WebSocket connections.

docs.title: Try the endpoint
docs.text:
Start the application:

APPLICATION_ENVIRONMENT=develop go run ./cmd/myapp serve

Open http://127.0.0.1:8080/docs and run this in the browser's developer console:

const socket = new WebSocket("ws://127.0.0.1:8080/ws/echo");
socket.onopen = () => socket.send("hello");
socket.onmessage = (event) => console.log(event.data);
socket.onclose = (event) => console.log("closed", event.code, event.reason);

The console prints hello. Stop the server with Ctrl+C while the socket is open; the client receives close code 1001. To close from the client instead, run socket.close(1000, "done").

docs.title: Messages and handshake errors
docs.text:
After the HTTP 101 upgrade, messages use your application's WebSocket protocol; Zodiac does not add the JSON response envelope. Authentication or other business checks can return an error from the registered handler before returning the StreamResponse. Errors written by websocket.Accept, such as an invalid handshake, use that library's HTTP response format.

The example keeps the library's same-origin check. If your browser client is hosted elsewhere, configure AcceptOptions.OriginPatterns with its allowed hosts. See AcceptOptions.
